title: synchronized, volatile & the Java Memory Model
html:
Shared mutable state + more than one thread = a race. synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility; volatile gives visibility and ordering only.

Race condition — the result depends on the timing of threads. The classic case is count++, which is really three steps — read, add 1, write — so two threads can read the same old value and one increment is lost.

The lost-update problem

The fix: synchronized

Every object has an intrinsic lock (monitor). Only one thread at a time can hold it; others trying to enter a synchronized region on the same object go BLOCKED.

FormLock usedUse when
synchronized void m()thisThe whole method touches shared state
static synchronized void m()the Class object (Main.class)Guarding static fields
synchronized (lock) { ... }any object you chooseOnly a few lines need the lock — keep critical sections short
Watch out

An instance lock and a static lock are different locks: a synchronized instance method and a static synchronized method can run at the same time. Also, locking on different objects protects nothing — every access to the shared field must use the same lock.

Reentrancy

Intrinsic locks are reentrant: the JVM keeps a hold count per owning thread, so a synchronized method can call another synchronized method on the same object.

Visibility and the Java Memory Model

Without synchronisation, a thread may never see another thread's write: values can sit in CPU caches or registers, and the compiler/CPU may reorder instructions. The Java Memory Model (JMM) defines when a write is guaranteed visible through happens-before rules.

Happens-before ruleGuarantee
Program orderEach action in a thread happens-before later actions in the same thread
Monitor lockUnlocking a monitor happens-before every later lock of the same monitor
volatileA write to a volatile field happens-before every later read of it
Thread startt.start() happens-before anything t does
Thread joinEverything t does happens-before t.join() returns
TransitivityA hb B and B hb C ⇒ A hb C

volatile

volatilesynchronized
VisibilityYesYes
Prevents reordering around itYesYes
Atomic compound actions (x++, check-then-act)NoYes
Blocks other threadsNeverYes (mutual exclusion)
Typical useStatus flags, safe publication, DCLInvariants spanning several fields/steps
Watch out

volatile int count; count++ is still a race — volatile makes each read and write visible but does not make read-modify-write atomic. Use synchronized, AtomicInteger or LongAdder.

Double-checked locking (lazy singleton)

Without volatile, the write of the reference could be reordered before the constructor finishes, so another thread might see a partially constructed object. Simpler alternatives: an enum singleton or the holder idiom (private static class Holder { static final Config I = new Config(); }) — class initialisation is already thread-safe and lazy.

Is count++ atomic in Java?

No — it compiles to read, add, write (getfield, iadd, putfield). Two threads can interleave and lose updates, even if count is volatile. Use synchronized, AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() or LongAdder.

What does volatile guarantee?

Visibility (a read sees the latest write by any thread) and ordering (no reordering across the volatile access; it creates a happens-before edge). It does not give atomicity or mutual exclusion.

Synchronized method vs synchronized block?

A synchronized method locks this (or the Class for static methods) for the whole method. A block lets you choose the lock object — often a private final field — and keep the critical section as small as possible, which improves throughput and prevents outside code from locking on your object.

Why must the double-checked-locking field be volatile?

instance = new Config() is allocate → construct → assign, and the JIT/CPU may publish the reference before construction completes. volatile forbids that reordering, so a thread that sees a non-null reference also sees a fully initialised object.
